The change in perspective turned their attitudes towards the paths their great-great-grandmother had planned out for them right around — instead of being skulky and pouty at the idea of religious work, the two of them took to it like ducks to water, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship |and how so ]." But perhaps I did nudge it a bit early on, so that the effects are much more pronounced down the line." |Has she any comment on the twins' particular afflictions? "To be honest? No, not really[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Everyone who's banished here has a reason for said banishment, and even the colonial-born often if not always bear some kind of slight dysfunction in the bloodline. When everyone is troubled, disturbed or otherwise not working quite right, no one is. That's the beauty of the colonies, or so the joke goes — you don't feel awkward or weird if most people around you have a problem that's just as bad as yours, if not worse." That's a pretty blunt way to put it; she makes her home sound like some kind of leper colony. Hotaru chuckles, although there's no humor in it. "Well, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, ]we must be light cases in this analogy, for the severe ones don't even make it here to begin with. "But to circle back to the point, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence, ]no. Miko and Mai are simply who they are. Of course, some people love any reason to gossip, but I'd like to imagine that I'm just a little more sanguine than that." |Is it true that Miko can actually see the future? "I've never known her to tell a wrong fortune, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship |that much I know ]. If Miko can unerringly tell the future, [pc.bg scholar acolyte minstrel noblescion |then doesn't that raise questions about fate, whether one's actions matter, and of the nature of free will |then isn't that a little creepy? ]这是不可避免的，而且她越是推迟戒掉那种药物，情况只会变得越糟。必须得采取行动，也许不必用这种方式，但任何能够让她戒掉那种毒瘾的方法，都会带来同样痛苦，甚至更痛苦。哦，太疼了……你记得得太清楚了。你当时还在想发生了什么，是否能够帮忙，结果下一刻，她就冲到你面前，用爪子抓你，同时还试图用她的体重压断你的髋骨。 萤轻轻眨了眨眼，微微低下了头。“其实，我所了解的只是些第二手甚至第三手部的传闻而已，所以如果有什么误解的话，请大家指正我。[pc.ra kitsune |我的[pc.mf |领主 |女士 ]运输 ]但据我了解，所有相关人员都被这些接连发生的事件卷入了一场巨大的漩涡之中……让我有点惊讶的是，尽管米可与舞拥有许多有趣的能力，但她们在各自的未来预测中都没有预见到这件事会发生。或许，因为他们早就知道这种事情会发生，所以两人都没有选择采取任何行动……对于那些深受其害的人来说，试图反抗这样的预感只会让事情变得更加糟糕。 对于所有相关的人来说，包括你，在这种态度存在的情况下，一切都会显得非常方便。这不过是宇宙中的不公平，以及生存本身所带来的苦难罢了。对于发生的事情，没有人应该受到责备——你当然也不例外——因此大家应该把注意力放在接下来该做什么上，而不是互相指责。 “就这样吧。[pc.ra kitsune |我的[pc.mf |领主 |女士 ]运输 ]你终于开始理解在这里处理这类棘手问题时应该采取的正确态度了。” 萤吐了吐舌头，摇了摇头。“尽管一开始情况很棘手，但最终结果还算不错，所以大多数人都选择不再追究这件事了。 |这些天，舞不再整天整夜地散发着冬茎烟的味道，和她在一起真的容易多了。[pc.ra kitsune |，阁下 ]萤说道，‘虽然可以从这种植物中提取出非常优质的染料——这也是我唯一会为失去舞培育的那些品种而感到遗憾的原因——但就我个人而言，我并不喜欢用它来放松身心。那种气味实在让我无法忍受…… 正如你所了解的，早在神战之前，甚至可能更早的时候，边境地区的居民就已经开始将冬茎这种植物用于娱乐性吸烟了。这个地区的原住民——狼族族和极北精灵们——从远古时代起，就将这种行为视为他们文化中不可或缺的一部分。 点了点头。“她最初就是通过这种方式了解到这种药物的——有一位当地的慈善家恰好拥有一些这种药物。她原本也是打算像米可一样接受同样的精神训练，后来才设法得到了这些种子。……冬季茎这种植物在人工环境下极其难以培育，不过当地人却掌握了对其进行侧向整形的技术。[pc.ra kitsune |，阁下 ]舞采到了足够的药材，足以支撑她度过接下来的一段时间，但情况从那以后反而变得更糟了。” 而现在，这一切都已经结束了。 “事情本来也不可能有其他结局。 [pc.ra kitsune |我的[pc.mf |领主 |女士 ]运输 |恐怕不行。 ]现在她有了孩子，所以在可预见的未来，她永远也无法再养成那个习惯了。从长远来看，这一切对舞来说都会是有益的，但在那之前，我们只能尽我们所能来应对她这种情绪不稳定的情况了。 |所以……萤确实是一个充满想象力、擅长讲故事的人，对吧？ “希望真是这样。[pc.ra kitsune |，阁下 ]我当然认为自己就是这样的人。” 那么，就你们俩之间来说……假设舞揭露自己与冬茎有关的秘密这件事并非偶然，而是有人故意策划的；她错误地减少了用药剂量，以及之后发生的一切，其实都是某人一手造成的。在她看来，谁会是那种假设情境中的犯罪者呢？ “显然，我会把怀疑对象指向她的直系亲属。林多或许会怀有足够的同情心，而且与舞的关系也足够亲密，因此有可能有这样的动机，但她性格比较被动，也没有足够的决心去采取如此极端的行动。 类似的情况当然也适用于军事检察官。毫无疑问，他一定认为自己那些亲戚的行为令人愤慨。[pc.ra kitsune |，阁下 ]他们是神的仆从，因此他无权指责他们。而且，这种阴险的手段也不是他的作风。所以，动机是存在的，但除此之外没有别的原因。 “那个巢穴的女头目肯定有能力、动机，也愿意将这样的行动付诸实施——她显然也不愿意进一步探究这件事是如何发生在她的后裔身上的。然而，鉴于在那种情况下她对舞的愤怒情绪已经消退，再加上她表现出的沮丧之情是真实的，而以她的经验，她本来是不会冒那种风险的。另外，还有一个问题：她为什么要等到那么久才采取这样的行动？其实，她完全有能力直接禁止舞使用那种药物。 那就只剩下米可了。她就是这个意思吗？ 热灯无助地耸了耸肩：“动机吗……米可做任何事都需要动机吗？机会嘛，她拥有任何人都可能用来干扰她妹妹的机会。而且她确实足够肆无忌惮，会不顾及任何人或任何事情就去做这件事。我并不是说有什么证据可以用来指控她。[pc.ra kitsune |我的[pc.mf |领主 |女士 ]运输 ]但如果你问我，事情就会发展成那样。要么就是舞太粗心了，弄错了用药剂量，这种情况其实比你想象的要常见得多。 ]
rows.raw: " [var0 |Since she says she was born here... how long have Miko and Mai been shrine maidens? "They arrived when they were six — although I was too young to remember that particular event — and started working at the shrine at ten[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Before that, there'd been a period of time when the den matron was manning the shrine herself and had set up a temporary office in the nearby gazebo, if you can call a period of years temporary. Strictly speaking, ten is a little too young to start taking on those spiritual duties in, but the sisters were anything but normal, nor are the practices orthodox inasmuch as anything of that kind can be called orthodox..." Miko and Mai also had an excellent tutor. "Just so[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. The den matron may often joke about needing something to fill in all the hours of the day someone normal might spend on eating, sleeping, and all those other humdrum activities, but I think she was getting tired of working two jobs at once. A normal person certainly wouldn't have been able to maintain that kind of schedule... "But yes[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]! They've been at this for a long time. One would expect them to be promoted to priestesses sometime soon, but frankly they're already serving that purpose and it's not like there's any other religious authority in the colonies save for the den matron herself, is there? They'd have to change their uniforms, too, and as the person who'd have to make said garments, I think they look better with their current getup." |You've been wondering — since she's been around for a little while, was she the one who put together Miko and Mai's outfits? "Strictly speaking, no; they wanted to sew them together with their own hands. But a me of fifteen or sixteen summers certainly had an outsized influence on how the uniforms eventually turned out, given that they came to me for advice quite often." And whose idea was it to make their uniforms unorthodox? Hotaru smiles sweetly. "That would be me, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |of course ]. Not that the sisters took any convincing after I brought up the idea, but still, if I hadn't, they might've wound up being boring. The change in perspective turned their attitudes towards the paths their great-great-grandmother had planned out for them right around — instead of being skulky and pouty at the idea of religious work, the two of them took to it like ducks to water, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship |and how so ]." Might she have changed the entire trajectory of the twins' future? "Oh, I wouldn't give myself such airs[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. But perhaps I did nudge it a bit early on, so that the effects are much more pronounced down the line." |Has she any comment on the twins' particular afflictions? "To be honest? No, not really[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Everyone who's banished here has a reason for said banishment, and even the colonial-born often if not always bear some kind of slight dysfunction in the bloodline. When everyone is troubled, disturbed or otherwise not working quite right, no one is. That's the beauty of the colonies, or so the joke goes — you don't feel awkward or weird if most people around you have a problem that's just as bad as yours, if not worse." That's a pretty blunt way to put it; she makes her home sound like some kind of leper colony. Hotaru chuckles, although there's no humor in it. "Well, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, ]we must be light cases in this analogy, for the severe ones don't even make it here to begin with. And if it's to be a sickness, it's one that's borne by the blood, because even those who're born on this soil are afflicted in some way. "But to circle back to the point, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence, ]no. Miko and Mai are simply who they are. They have their afflictions which have the potential to manifest in a more public and dangerous manner, but there's not much to be said about it. We bear our burdens as best as we can. Of course, some people love any reason to gossip, but I'd like to imagine that I'm just a little more sanguine than that." |Is it true that Miko can actually see the future? "I've never known her to tell a wrong fortune, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship |that much I know ]. And she doesn't do the usual tricks charlatans do like reading people, being vague and letting people fill in the blanks themselves, that sort of thing. When we were younger, she told me that I'd be hit in the shoulder by a falling branch three days in advance, and rubbed the spot where I'd be struck. Despite me doing everything to avoid it, I was struck in the end, and on the very same spot." If Miko can unerringly tell the future, [pc.bg scholar acolyte minstrel noblescion |then doesn't that raise questions about fate, whether one's actions matter, and of the nature of free will |then isn't that a little creepy? Like things are fated and nothing you do matters ]? Hotaru shrugs. "To be frank, that's too [silly |big-brained |intellectual ] for me. That being said, Old Country mythology is full of that kind of thing — fate, hubris, and the people who try and defy the former. It never goes well for almost all of them. And so you learn one of the reasons why 'nothing can be done about it' is a very common aphorism[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]" She said almost, so there are exceptions? "We aren't all necessarily bound to the same degree, or in the same way. There are also incredibly rare people over whom the grand kami time, fate and death has no hold over... but if Miko can see your future, you're unfortunately not one of them. The first emperor Belhar was supposedly one of these people, but none of us are to be so fortunate — or unfortunate, depending on your point of view. "But yes[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Miko doesn't give fortunes that aren't accurate. If she says it's coming, it's coming on the exact time and in the exact way that she said. If she doesn't know, then she'll say as much. It may be small, but knowing the exact weather tomorrow is important to the point where she just puts up a sign by the donation box with the exact schedule. Really helps with planning, and encourages people to drop by and be pious while checking out the next day's forecast." |"Oh, their accent? I've never had a problem with it[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. Maybe it's just because I'm used to it, but Miko and Mai's accent has never been any impediment to me understanding them." Would it be that you were so fortunate. Most of it you can get, but the sisters' speech can get pretty thick in places and that's on top of the fact that Belharan is not their native language. "Truth be told, I quite like it[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Most accents gradually fall away when one spends more and more company with others who speak differently, but the sisters have kept their way of speaking all this time. That's quite the achievement, when you think about it. Not that they faced serious direct pressure to change it, but still. It's part of who they are at this point." |"I guess it finally happened, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence, |didn't it? ]" Hotaru says with a lazy flick of her ears. "We all knew it was coming someday and it was just a matter of time before the narrative of the situation caught up with reality. At least now everyone can drop the pretense that there was ever any kind of serious competition for the position of the den matron's heir, and there's no need to keep up appearances." That sentiment is probably why people aren't as upset as you imagined they'd be, what with the kitsune being as stereotypically uptight as they are. Everyone was waiting for the proverbial shoe to drop, weren't they? A nod. "They were[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. It's not as if it makes much of a difference, since neither sister makes any kind of important decision without consulting the other. But as someone who tells stories, I know that words, names and titles have power, and it's a relief to be able to stop pretending and be able to speak straight." Even knowing all this, it doesn't feel like the impact upon Miko has lessened any. Maybe it's just you, but... "[pc.ra kitsune |With all due respect, your Eminence, ]I really don't see it. The den matron's the only one who's seriously upset about this. What people say is one thing, how they act is another, and it's the latter that counts." |"It's ridiculous, isn't it?" What is? "How Miko absolutely swelled up while with child,[pc.ra kitsune | your Eminence, ] Hotaru says with a giggle. "You did such an absolute number on her that I'm actually a bit envious. Despite her absolutely ballooning up, and not just in front, she didn't put on that much fat — so much of it was just solid meat." Well, anyone who took a look at her while she was carrying your kits would've found it obvious... "But [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, ]I have an extremely detailed account of it all given how many adjustments poor Miko needed throughout it all. She was coming to me far too often just to be able to keep up with her body... but seeing her all flustered like that was worth all the sleepless nights. I kept a record of all her body measurements, and several sketches... would you like to see them[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]? I've never seen anything like it in all my life. I don't know if it's related to her particular affliction, but it's almost as if she was soaking in chi like a sponge, her childbearing an excuse for her to become absolutely impregnated through and through with life essence." All right, now you're pretty sure that Hotaru's teasing you. Is she even telling the truth about keeping Miko's measurements to begin with? "As a matter of course, I do so for just about everyone who lives here[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. Makes my work easier, you see. But poor Miko... ah, I had to re-take them every time she came in, and even with me making them a little loose she still was a regular visitor. I think even the den matron was surprised, and that's saying something." Oh, right. What was that she was saying about being envious earlier, anyway? Hotaru meets your jab with a small smile and raises her vivid red eyes to meet yours. "I meant every word of what I said[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Anyone else who put on even half of that much weight in a fraction of the time would start spilling all over the place, but not Miko. She remained nice and tight...mostly. I swear, the whole situation would be absolutely unbelievable if I didn't have such an intimate experience out of it all — I think I'll be cooking up a great story out of it, ehe." |"Oh, Mikoto," Hotaru says, heaving a sigh so deep her bosom visibly rises and falls under all the clothing she's wearing. "Poor, poor Mikoto. Still a child in the head, and already having children of her own. If it weren't for the den matron and her sister, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, ]I'd be more worried for her. As things are, though, I'm just content to tease. "I expect many more amusing but ultimately harmless antics from her in the years to come, especially if the kits take after her when it comes to playfulness[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Maybe she'll finally learn that her cavalier attitude to just about anything and everything isn't so funny when one's on the receiving end." |"On one hand, seeing Mai go through all of this is heartbreaking and more than a little necessary. On the other, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence, ] it was inevitable, and was only going to get worse the longer she put off being weaned from that drug of hers. It had to be done, maybe not in this exact manner, but anything sufficient to get her to kick that pipe habit of hers would've been just as painful if not more." Oh, painful... you remember that all too clearly. You were wondering what was going on and if you could help, and next thing you know she's in your face clawing at you while trying to break your hips under hers at the same time. Hotaru flicks a hear and bows her head slightly. "Now, I've only second if not third-hand accounts of what happened, so please do correct me if there's been a misunderstanding[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. But as I understand things, everyone involved has been swept up in quite the whirlwind of events that just happened to occur as they did... I'm mildly surprised that for all the interesting things that Miko and Mai can do, neither of them saw this coming in either of their own futures. Or maybe, knowing that it was going to happen, neither of them decided to do anything about it... for those so afflicted, attempting to defy such visions just makes things worse." It's very convenient for everyone involved, you included, that this sort of attitude exists. It's just cosmic injustice and the misery inherent to existence, no one's to blame for what happened — you certainly aren't — and everyone can focus on what to do next instead of pointing fingers. "Just so[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]; you're really starting to comprehend the appropriate mindset in which prickly matters are approached around these parts." Hotaru clicks her tongue and shakes her head. "Despite its rocky start, the whole matter has turned out for the best, so most are content to just leave it be." |"It's much easier to be around Mai these days now that she doesn't have the stench of winterstem smoke clinging to her day and night[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]," Hotaru says. "While an excellent dye can be extracted from the plant — the only reason I would possibly bemoan the loss of Mai's cultivars — I personally don't enjoy its use as a relaxant. Can't stand the smell..." As you understand it, winterstem's been smoked for fun by the people of the Marches since before the Godswar, perhaps even before then. The original natives of this region — the lupines and boreal elves — certainly consider it part of their culture since time immemorial. A nod. "That's how she learned of the drug in the first place — a local benefactor who happened to have some. She was originally going to undergo the same mental training regimen as Miko, then managed to get her hands on some seeds... winterstem is notoriously hard to raise in captivity, but the locals don't have the art of shaping on their side[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Mai was able to harvest enough medicinal herbs to keep her going till the next, and it just got worse from there." And that whole business is over now. "It could have ended no other way, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship |I'm afraid ]. And now that she has a child, she'll never be able to pick up the habit for the foreseeable future. All of this will be better for Mai in the long run, but until that happens we just have to do what we can with her being as volatile as she is." |So... Hotaru is a rich storyteller with a vivid imagination, isn't she? "I would hope that's the case[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. I certainly fancy myself as such." Then, just between the both of you... let's say that this whole business with Mai coming clean of winterstem wasn't an accident, but deliberately engineered by someone; that her cutting her dose wrongly and all the things that followed were the hand of someone. Who, in her estimation, would be the perpetrators of that hypothetical situation? "For obvious reasons, I'd cast my eye upon her immediate family. Rindo might feel enough compassion and be close enough to Mai to have the motivation for such an act, but she's a passive creature and wouldn't have the will to see through such drastic action. "Something similar would certainly apply to the military provost. While he no doubt founds the behavior of his cousins deplorable[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ], they are servants of the divine and hence it's beyond him to reproach them. That, and this kind of underhanded means isn't his type. So, motive, but nothing else. "The den matron would certainly have the means, motive and will to see such an act through — she certainly was disinclined to inquire further into how this happened to her descendant. However, her anger at the circumstances under Mai was taken off the drug leads me to believe she didn't do it; her dismay was genuine and someone with her experience wouldn't have taken that kind of risk. That, and the question remains as to why she would've waited so long before taking such a step; it would've been well within her ability to outright forbid her from the drug. That leaves Miko. Is that what she's saying? Hotaru gives you a helpless shrug. "Motive... does Miko need a motive for anything she does? Opportunity — she's got every chance anyone would ever need to mess with her sister. And she's certainly cavalier enough to do it without consideration for anyone or anything. I'm not saying that there's any evidence to make any kind of accusation[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ], but if you asked me, that's how it'd shake out. Either that, or Mai was careless and messed up her dosage, happens more often than you'd think." ] "

rows.original: [var0 |"I wonder if it's some cruel joke played upon the girl that she dresses as she does," Hotaru says, looking contemplative and tapping her chin. "A poor soul with anywhere from a third to half of her body looking like seared beef, and she chooses to wear flame-patterned skirts. Oh, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, ]she well and truly is either amazingly resilient in having come to terms with her situation and making peace with it, or someone is having a laugh at her expense, even if it's the cosmos itself." ...Well, that's true, but no one's ever really called attention to it before.[silly | Well, maybe her outfit has good stats? Many people will eagerly become walking fashion disasters if it means a couple more points of attack. ] "Oh, trust me[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. People notice how you dress, people notice how the den matron and her great-great-granddaughters dress, people notice how anyone and everyone dresses even if they don't know it themselves. It's a state of affairs that I enjoy, because I like to think that I, in some small fashion, am influencing the lives of dozens of people who put on the clothes I create. Maybe Rindo does it on purpose, it is very poetic in a sad way." |"Rindo makes me feel very comfy with who I am," Hotaru says with a forced chuckle. "[pc.ra kitsune |My [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship... i |I ]t's nice to have just a drop or two of divinity in your veins, isn't it? Enough to feel special and smug about the circumstances of your birth, not enough to wind up like poor Rindo, torn from the life she'd been expected to lead because someone painted a huge marker on her back by naming her after the flower on the crest of the clan she was supposed to marry into. Under certain circumstances, there can indeed be too much of a good thing." So, people don't really worry about kitsune having red eyes? "It's the most minor of likenesses in resemblance to the August Master at the Center of Heaven[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Not exactly everyday amongst the common-born like humble me, but perhaps traceable to a distant ancestor. Facial markings are harder to explain away in such a manner... and white fur gets you into trouble. But all three at once? No, that is no coincidence[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ] — she is someone's by-blow, and a direct offshoot at that. I wonder why the tack suddenly changed from bringing her into the fold to trying to get rid of her — it would make for an excellent court drama, if nothing else — but it is something that we will almost certainly never know for sure." Hotaru herself, though... she's right. It's just enough to feel smug at being born just that bit special, but not enough to make herself a target, or to be saddled with responsibilities she doesn't want. "With all due respect[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]..." Smiling, Hotaru leans in and stage-whispers to you. "I really do feel very, very pretty as I am." |"I remember the day when I first set eyes on the poor girl in question, [pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. She'd just come in not too long ago and heard I was raising moths... she wanted to know how good they were at pollinating the flowers in the sacred gardens. I had to explain very carefully to her that silkworm moths are domesticated to the point where they can't fly any more, so they weren't about to do any pollination. Girl looked pretty sad at that." She didn't find Rindo's appearance odd or shocking? Hotaru shrugs. "All kinds of people come through the torii gate, none of whom you could describe as normal. But yes, I think she's as safe as can be. While the den matron is known as a cursed and unaging monster, she also traveled with the August Master at the Center of Heaven for many years. Both fear and grudging respect... it's as best a shield for Rindo as can be pulled together at short notice.[pc.ra kitsune |" |"That being said..." Yes? A frown mars Hotaru's delicate features. "The military provost's ambitions may prove to be problematic, but I don't think it should be a problem. The simple fact that he's colonial-born means that those whom he desperately wants to please will never accept anything he does as worthwhile, even if it were to be something earth-shattering. "No... never mind that I said anything. It's impossible that he would be viewed as a threat to anyone who would have problems with Rindo. Perhaps I've been spending too much time with my period court dramas." ] |"The important thing in all of this is that Rindo can continue to live her life with as little interruption as possible, which she has more or less achieved. I think most would agree that the girl's had just about enough excitement to last a lifetime, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |maybe more ]. With her having married into the colonial governor's clan and the young lady Otomo looking to take her on as a retainer down the line, things are looking good. Better than they'd be otherwise." Is she sure about that? "Barring extenuating circumstances... this is about as happy an ending as real stories get[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. Asking for more might jinx it." She smiles, just a trace of sadness on her lips. "How sweet it truly can be when folktales come true, am I not right?" |"I think it'll be good for Rindo's continued cultural growth that the den matron decided to wed her to the military provost. He's one of the few people in these parts who's serious about cultural pursuits and has the means to pursue them in earnest — Rindo did tell me that she did enjoy her education when she was younger[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Perhaps now the opportunity will reopen itself, and with someone to share that interest with." Isn't Nakano absolutely terrible at poetry, though? "There are other cultural pursuits to expand the mind and deepen the soul other than poetry[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. The military provost is actually quite passable at them — although it's my hope that his newlywed wife will be able to help him with his long form poetry, too." Hotaru sighs. "I see the demand for mulberry paper going up in the future, along with more sleepless nights for me. A small price to pay, I suppose." |"Ahaha. You should've seen Rindo when she came in here about her wedding dress[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ] — she was just beaming all over the place. And she had every right to be, given that it was a dream come true for her; it's about time something good happened to the poor girl for once." Oh? Did she design Rindo's wedding dress, too? "If only I had that kind of time and expense to spare, I would've loved to do so, and you'd think that the colonial governor would at least spare that expense for her descendant's wedding," Hotaru replies with a wistful sigh. "But no[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ], it would be a waste of limited resources for little more than the indulgence of the governor's own. So, as these things go, Rindo wore the very same wedding dress that the colonial governor did more than two centuries ago." Oh, you've heard of these things. A heirloom that's been around that it's begun to fall apart, so one piece needs to get patched in, and another, and another, until there's no material at all from the original piece. And yet, despite the fixes over the years, it's still the very same item that was in use by some illustrious ancestor. Hotaru's smile turns mischievous. "Now you're getting the true essence of how stories work[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. But yes, it was the den matron's very own, and since Rindo is a lot more willowy than most of those who'd worn it before her, it had to be temporarily tucked in at several places. Not that she minded, of course, she was so happy at finally being able to stop pining over what she wanted and make something of what she now has. Isn't that sweet?" You had the chance to take Rindo for yourself as your concubine and passed it up; at least knowing that this outcome isn't so bad after all lessens any sting that said rejection might've had for you. Yes... at the very least, there's no need to regret your decision; Nakano might be insufferable to you, but he'll take good care of her. |"I think it'll be good for the military provost that he and Rindo are finally married," Hotaru says with a small smile. "It's generally considered not done for a warrior to be overambitious — Macahn ascetics say that ambition is one of the main sources of attachment, and attachment brings suffering to the self and others. That particular philosophy crept over to us many centuries ago, and if you're a local ruler you really don't want your enforcers getting too uppity, as it were." Nakano, ambitious? Perhaps, but as insufferable as he is, you really don't see him getting 'uppity', as Hotaru would put it. "It's...how should I put it[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" Hotaru pauses her needlework and snaps her fingers. "It's like that thing where you let someone believe he or she's really in charge, but you're guiding said person into doing what you want anyway. I don't think he's conscious of it himself and really does believe he's serving his obligations to family, nobility, and the gods to the utmost. "But back to the point. At least now that he has people beyond himself to live for, maybe he'll mellow out a bit." You're not entirely sure about that. Before he was wed to Rindo, Nakano still had his immediate family around to be concerned with — what's Rindo and a son going to do that Komari or Miko and Mai can't? "Hope springs eternal[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. Hopefully, he'll be able to find another meaningful direction in life. Or maybe not. But at least an opportunity has opened up, has it not? Having a wife and son is a fundamentally different relationship, I feel. If nothing else, it'd make for a good story." |Hotaru shifts her eyes from side to side, then leans in to whisper conspiratorially. "Have you seen what's happened to Rindo's body ever since she had a child[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" Yes, you have. You very much have... "Gods forbid. She used to be such a slip of a girl, and just absolutely blew up like a... like a... something that blows up as much as that. I had to see it, and even then I couldn't quite believe it." Hotaru chuckles dryly, and folds her ears forward. "Just one kit did that to her... can you imagine if she were to have another[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]? Letting all of her clothes out to fit her new measurements... it's as if all the time spent in the colonies was just being put away, and it all came out to plump her up in the blink of an eye. I'm not so desperate as to want to get pregnant just to have that for myself, but it's still truly impressive! "But the best part is — and I don't think she's noticed it herself — that when she smiles, she does so in a manner that we call 'up to one's eyes'[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. As much as someone like me should know better about the value of appearances, it's still extremely nice to see." |"It's interesting, [pc.ra kitsune |my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship. |don't you think? ] What is? "Before she had a kit, Rindo used to walk with a very slight stiffness on hm, that side of her body. You know what I mean[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Whether it be from the tightness and hardening of the skin on that side of her or a more internal injury, it was there if barely perceptible. Only reason I know it's there is that I've known her ever since the day she set foot in the den. "And now... after she's carried a child in her womb, that stiffness is gone. It's amazing." Call you skeptical, but it makes more sense that Rindo's contentment with this new direction in her life has inspired more energy and a spring in her step, rather than any miraculous healing caused by her pregnancy. Hotaru purses her lips, sets down her needle and folds her arms. "[pc.ra kitsune |With all due respect, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship, I don't think it's as far-fetched as one might imagine. |Boo, you're no fun ]. Her body's certainly had a glow-up from head to toe; there's little doubt that her next child will be easier on her than the first one was. Is it really that much of a flight of fancy to imagine that it fixed a minor if long-lasting wound?" Not necessarily, but you think it's more sappy if the wound was on her heart instead of her body. "Oooooooh. I still think I prefer my story, though. The act of her carrying a child conceived in love being powerful enough to reach into the realm of the physical and mend where every other attempt failed... that's more heart-warming[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]." Well, you'll just have to agree to disagree on that. |"Have you seen how absolutely adorable Rindo's son is? Such a quiet and well-behaved little thing, just like his mother. I was speaking with Rindo the other day when she came in to deliver some dyes from the artificer, and she had her kit slung over her back in a little bundle. Absolutely adorable, and no fuss at all. If only all babies were this docile..." Like mother, like son. That being said, it's better that the kit resemble his mother on the inside than on the outside, and you don't mean Rindo's scars by that. Hotaru swallows hard. "Oh. Oh no, of course not[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ]. Someone like that is bad enough for stability. But for two generations in a row? No, the ocean would not be enough to ensure a peaceful life for the child. It's for the best that he's as dissimilar to his mother in appearance as these things come." ] "

rows.original: Hotaru thinks a moment, then nods. "[pc.ra kitsune |I am more than willing to oblige, your Eminence |Sure, I need to keep my mouth moving anyway ]. "[rand |Long ago, there was a noble and righteous judge who was much loved by the people. One day, his magistrate understudy came up to him and asked: 'My lordship, how do you keep in favor with the emperor so consistently despite the workings of the court? Certainly you have angered many powerful people in your doings — how is it that you keep in his good graces, and hence his protection?" The judge considered his understudy, then replied to her: 'do you enjoy festival sweets?' 'Well, yes, my lordship.' The magistrate's reply was polite, but her hesitation betrayed her confusion. 'I'm truly looking forward to this summer for the chance to sample them again.' 'Could you have them every day, though?' 'No, the flavor is undoubtedly too rich. To have them every day... that would certainly make one ill.' 'And what of rice, then? What is so special about it that everyone has it everyday, without so much as thinking?' 'There is nothing special or noteworthy about it, my lordship. It simply fills the belly and keeps one going.' Several moments passed while the judge waited to see if his understudy would grasp the analogy, and when she did not he sighed and explained it to her. 'See, now. Every day, the emperor is plied not just by the twelve den mothers, but everyone in his court with the sweetest of deceptions. They may entertain him for a little while, but the empty compliments and transparent self-interest has him soon tiring of them; festival sweets are for the tongue and not the body. 'Yet I, with his permission, lay the simple truth before him when I am summoned to court. Like plain rice, it is not particularly exciting or tasteful, but my words are useful to him and he trusts me to give an honest assessment of any question he asks of me; in turn, I find that he reaches for my counsel as unthinkingly as people have rice every meal.'" Having finished her tale, Hotaru sets down her needle, steeples her fingers and smiles at you. "So, your thoughts about this tale[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" Sounds a bit contrived, but you understand that it's trying to get across a moral lesson.[pc.bg noblescion | You're well aware that in the world of aristocrats, it's not just as simple as telling the truth... ] "Mm. There is something I've noticed when looking over old Belharan tales and comparing them to that of my home nation. Where public officials are involved in folklore, those who star in tales were wicked ones who abandoned their duty. On the other hand, tales from across the ocean are of noble and righteous officials who at least tried to uphold the ideals of their station. "It says something about the times and places where these legends originated and the kinds of people they considered noteworthy[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. In old Belhar, people expected civil servants to at least try to do their jobs right. Not that it was necessarily the actual case, but the expectation was there, and wicked officials were considered noteworthy and enshrined in legend. On the other hand, righteous civil servants from my homeland were considered noteworthy of being immortalised in tales... which implies that people simply expected corruption and took it in stride if they were to meet with it." That... "Beautiful as it was, the period preceding the shogunate was a bit of a mess." Hotaru's smile turns sad. "I'd like to think we've learned something in all these centuries, to be in such a strong position compared to the other nations today. But there you have it[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ] — a story for you." |This one's not from my homeland, but from neighboring Macah; nevertheless, I think it's a good enough story to tell. Long ago, there was a wicked prime minister in that land, who had installed a puppet emperor on the throne. Yet that was not good enough for him — said puppet emperor was chafing at his bonds due to a recent peasant uprising that was proving difficult to suppress, and not without reason blamed the prime minister for it. "Naturally, the wicked minister didn't like that, nor how uncooperative his puppet was becoming; he started to think that maybe there should be a change of emperor, but he couldn’t be sure he could pull it off. So he brought a deer into the palace by the horns, called the emperor to come out, and said: 'look, your majesty! I've brought you a fine horse!" "The emperor, not amused, replied: 'surely you are mistaken to be calling a deer a horse. Right?' "All the ministers in the court were on the edge of their seats; some were silently sweating nervously, while others loudly proclaimed what a fine horse this was. Great horse, look at this tail! These fine legs. Great horse, naturally the prime minister has the best of tastes. A handful did protest that this was a deer, not a horse; those were soon after summarily executed by some pretext or the other, and the emperor himself was mysteriously murdered some time later." Hotaru pauses a moment to let that all sink in, then shakes her head. "This story made it into the Records of the Grand Historian Sima Qian around three hundred years before the Godswar, through which it became part of common knowledge in Macahn intellectual life. From then on, every time somebody tried to pull off a similar stunt, opposing ministers could say 'you’re trying to say a deer is a horse, huh!.' That could either provoke other lukewarm ministers to wake up and support you... or get you killed with your whole family. "Such is the nature of these games[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Bringing in a pony and calling it a horse won’t do; someone might honestly mistake a horse for a pony. Only lies that are breathtakingly stupid, things no sane person could say or believe, are sufficient to serve as loyalty tests for the wicked." Hmm. You remember a similar Belharan story about a child and the emperor's new clothes. Has she heard of that one? A small sigh. "I indeed have[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ] — taking in the native folktales has been interesting for a number of reasons. Such a tale: a child, who having a pure heart, dares to speak the truth against the powerful; the moral is that we should be ashamed of ourselves, and aspire to be as virtuous as this child. But of course the folktale abruptly cuts off there, because this child would have been arrested and executed in moments, along with his parents. It's plain why nobody tells the emperor about his new clothes: they’re not stupid." Gods, kitsune are downright depressing when they want to be. [pc.isDK |But... it's hard to argue with the thrust of the argument. How many inane self-deceptions do people labor under just to get through the day, let alone lies forced upon them by those around and above? |That folktale's meant to push an ideal, and just because it may be considered unrealistic by some, or that people fall short of it, doesn't mean that the ideal is worthless. Whether it's a good ideal to pursue shouldn't factor in the so-called realities of existence. ] "It is simply a different perspective, and the results of both are plain for all to see." |In ancient days there lived in a remote part of Kitsuhon a man and his wife, and they were blessed with a little girl, who was much beloved of her parents. On one occasion the man was called away on business by the coast. Before he went he told his daughter that if she were good and dutiful to her mother, he would bring her back a present she would prize very highly. Then the good man took his departure, mother and daughter watching him go. "At last he returned to his home, and after his wife and child had taken off his large hat and sandals he sat down upon the white mats and opened a bamboo basket, watching the eager gaze of his little child. He took out a wonderful doll and a lacquer box of cakes and put them into her outstretched hands. Once more he reached into his basket, and presented his wife with a metal mirror; its smooth surface shone brightly, while upon its back there was a design of pine trees and storks. "The good man's wife had never seen a mirror before, and on gazing into it she was under the impression that another woman looked out upon her as she gazed with growing wonder. Her husband explained the mystery and bade her take great care of the mirror. "Not long after this happy homecoming and distribution of presents, the woman became very ill. Just before she died, she called to her little daughter, and said: 'dear child, take care of your father when I am gone. You will miss me when I have left you, but take this mirror, and when you feel most lonely look into it and you will always see me.' Having said these words, she passed away. "In due time the man married again, and his wife was not at all kind to her stepdaughter. But the little one, remembering her mother's words, would retire to a corner and eagerly look into the mirror, where it seemed to her that she saw her dear mother's face, not drawn in pain as she had seen it on her deathbed, but young and beautiful. "One day, this child's stepmother chanced to see her crouching in a corner over an object she could not quite see, murmuring to herself. This ignorant woman, who detested the child and believed that her stepdaughter detested her in return, fancied that this little one was performing some strange magical art. Full of these notions, the stepmother went to her husband and told him that his wicked child was doing her best to kill her by witchcraft. "When the master of the house had listened to this extraordinary claim, he went straight to his daughter's room. He took her by surprise, and immediately the girl saw him she slipped the mirror into her sleeve. For the first time her doting father grew angry, and he feared that there was, after all, truth in what his wife had told him, and he repeated her tale forthwith. "When his daughter had heard this unjust accusation she was amazed at her father's words, and she told him that she loved him far too well ever to attempt or wish to kill his wife, who she knew was dear to him. 'What have you hidden in your sleeve?' said her father, only half convinced and still much puzzled. 'The mirror you gave my mother, and which she on her deathbed gave to me. Every time I look into its shining surface I see the face of my dear mother, young and beautiful. When my heart aches — and oh! it has ached so much lately — I take out the mirror, and mother's face, with sweet, kind smile, brings me peace, and helps me to bear hard words and cross looks.' "Then the man understood and loved his child the more for her filial piety. Even the girl's stepmother, when she knew what had really taken place, was ashamed and asked forgiveness. And this child, who believed she had seen her mother's face in the mirror, forgave, and trouble forever departed from the home." Having recited the entire tale, Hotaru reaches for a sip of tea while you ponder what she's just told you. For once, at least, a tale from a fox that doesn't end in misery, death, or any kind of horrible tragedy for anyone involved whilst teaching an important moral lesson. Even the antagonist in this learns to be better and lives contentedly instead of being miserably and horribly punished in a cruel and unusual fashion. "Oh, there're plenty of those, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |believe me ]," Hotaru says, setting down her teacup and returning to her needlework. "But sometimes, a little escapism from all the cynicism can't hurt." |Once upon a time there lived two frogs, one of whom made his home in a ditch near the coast, while the other dwelt in a clear little stream which ran through the mountains. At such a great distance apart, they had never even heard of each other; but, funnily enough, the idea came into both their heads at once that they should like to see a little of the world, and the frog who lived by the coast wanted to visit the inland mountains, and the frog who lived in the mountains wished to go to the coast and see the ocean for himself. "So one fine morning in the spring they both set out along the road that led from the coast to the mountains, one from one end and the other from the other. The journey was more tiring than they expected, for they did not know much about traveling, and halfway between their destinations there arose a traveler's stop which boasted a tall pavilion. It so happened that they decided to both take a rest within the rooftop garden, and what was the surprise of each to see another frog before him! "Both frogs looked at each other for a moment without speaking, and then fell into conversation, explaining the cause of their meeting so far from their homes. It was delightful to find that they both felt the same wish — to learn a little more of their native country — and as there was no sort of hurry they stretched themselves out in a cool, damp place, and agreed that they could learn much from each other before they parted to go their ways. "'What a pity we are not bigger,' said the coastal frog; 'for then we could see our destinations from here, and tell if it is worth our while continuing our journeys.' "'Oh, that is easily managed,' replied the mountain frog. 'We have only to stand up on our hind legs and hold onto each other, and then we can each look at the town he is traveling to.' "This idea pleased the coastal frog so much that he at once jumped up and put his front paws on the shoulder of his friend, who had risen also. There they both stood, stretching themselves as high as they could, and holding each other tightly, so that they might not fall down. The mountain frog turned his nose towards the coast, and the coastal frog turned his nose towards the mountains; but the foolish creatures forgot that when they stood up their great eyes lay in the backs of their heads, and that though their noses might point to the places to which they wanted to go, their eyes beheld the places from which they had come. "'Dear me!' cried the coastal frog, 'the mountains are exactly like the ocean. It is certainly not worth such a long journey, I shall go home!' "'If I had any idea that the coast was so alike to the mountains I should never have traveled all this way!' exclaimed the frog from the mountains, and as he spoke he took his hands from his friend's shoulders, and they both fell down on the ground. Then they took a polite farewell of each other, and set off for home again, and to the end of their lives they believed that the ocean and the mountains, which are as different as can be, were as alike as two peas." Having finished her story, Hotaru sets down her needlework and reaches for a little tea to wet her lips, studying you with her vivid red eyes and clearly awaiting a response. Well, what's the moral of the story? "Is there necessarily one[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" No, a story doesn't necessarily need to have a learning message, but given her method of delivery and the language she used in telling it, you get the feeling that this folktale about a couple of frogs is supposed to impart some kind of important lesson. It's a fox folktale, after all. "Mm, new experiences are good and all, but in order to benefit the most one needs to approach the new knowledge from a fresh perspective as well. Unable to change the way they saw things, the frogs benefited very little from their journey[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. It's something to think about, and why I'm not particularly envious of those who travel." |Once, there was an old man named Takahama who lived in a little house behind a temple cemetery. He was extremely amiable and generally liked by his neighbors, though most of them considered him to be a little mad. His eccentricity, according to them, entirely rested upon the fact that he had never married or evinced desire for intimate companionship with anyone in all his years of life, preferring to remain a hermit. "One summer day he became very ill — so ill, in fact, that he sent for his sister and her son. Knowing that his neighbors considered him odd, they both came and did all they could to bring comfort during his last hours. While they watched, Takahama fell into a fevered asleep; but he had no sooner done so than a large white butterfly flew into the room and rested on the old man's pillow. His nephew tried to drive it away with a fan but it came back three times, loath to leave the sufferer. "At last Takahama's nephew chased it out into the garden, through the gate, and into the cemetery beyond, where it lingered over a woman's tomb, and then mysteriously disappeared. On examining the tomb the young man found the name 'Akiko' written upon it, together with a description narrating how Akiko died when she was eighteen. Though the tomb was covered with moss and must have been erected fifty years previously, the boy saw that it was surrounded with flowers, and that the little water tank had been recently filled. "When the young man returned to the house he found that his uncle had passed away, and he returned to his mother and told her what he had seen in the cemetery. "'Akiko?' replied his mother. 'When your uncle was young, he was betrothed to Akiko, but she died of consumption shortly before her wedding day. When Akiko left this world, your uncle resolved never to marry, and to live ever near her grave. For all these years he has remained faithful to his vow, and kept in his heart all the sweet memories of his one and only love. Every day he went to the cemetery, whether the air was fragrant with summer breeze or thick with falling snow; every day he went to her grave and prayed for her happiness, swept the tomb and set flowers there. When Takahama was dying, and he could no longer perform his loving task, Akiko came for him. That white butterfly was her sweet and loving soul.'" Having finished her tale, Hotaru gives you a quizzical look, then shakes her head. "There's no moral to be had here, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |I'm afraid ]. It's just one of those slightly sad stories that people tell over a fire or lantern late at night." You didn't say there ought to be... "Mm." ]
rows.translation: 萤思考了一会儿，然后点了点头。[pc.ra kitsune |我非常乐意效劳，阁下 |当然，反正我也得不停地说话才行 ]。 "[rand |很久以前，有一位高尚而正直的法官，他深受百姓的爱戴。有一天，他的法官助手走到他面前问道：“大人，尽管宫廷中充满了各种纷争，您却始终能够得到皇帝的青睐。在您的种种行为中，肯定得罪了许多有权势的人，那么您究竟是如何保持皇帝的欢心，从而获得他的保护的呢？ 法官考虑了一下他的助手，然后问她：“你喜欢节日的甜点吗？” “嗯，是的，大人。”法官的回答很礼貌，但她的语气中透露出些许犹豫，这暴露了她的困惑。“我真的非常期待今年夏天能再次品尝到这些甜点。 不过，能不能每天都吃呢？” “不行，这样的口味实在太浓烈了。如果每天都吃的话……肯定会让人生病的。” “那大米呢？大米有什么特别的之处，以至于大家都会每天吃它，而从不觉得有什么不妥呢？ 这并没有什么特别的或值得注意的地方，大人。它只不过是用来填饱肚子、让人能够继续活下去罢了。” 法官等待了片刻，想看看他的助手是否能够理解这个比喻；当她没有理解时，他叹了口气，便向她解释了起来。看吧，每天皇帝都会受到那些十二位贵妇以及宫廷中所有人的奉承与欺骗。这些虚伪的赞美和明显的私心虽然能让他暂时感到愉悦，但很快就会让他感到厌烦——节日的甜点不过是满足口腹之欲罢了，根本无法满足他的真正需求。 然而，在他允许的情况下，每当被召到法庭上时，我都会向他陈述那些朴实的真相。这些真相虽然并不特别引人注目，也不够生动有趣，但它们对他来说确实很有用，他也信任我能够对他提出的任何问题给出诚实的评估。反过来，我也发现，他寻求我的建议，就像人们每顿饭都离不开米饭一样，是一种自然而然的行为。 讲完故事后，萤将针放下，用手指轻轻按了按耳朵，然后对你笑了笑：“那么，你对这个故事有什么看法呢？[pc.ra kitsune |，阁下 ]？” 听起来有点刻意，但你也明白，这样做其实是想传达某种道德寓意吧。[pc.bg noblescion | 你很清楚，在贵族的世界里，说实话并没有那么简单…… ] kitsune |，阁下 ]在古老的贝尔哈尔，人们期望公务员至少能够尽力做好自己的工作。虽然实际情况未必总是如此，但人们至少是抱有这种期望的。预期值这样的例子确实存在，那些腐败的官员反而被认为值得被人们铭记，并被载入传说之中。而另一方面，我家乡那些正直的公务员，也会因为他们的美德而被载入故事中，被人们永远纪念……这说明，人们其实早已预料到腐败现象的存在，当遇到腐败时，也只会坦然接受罢了。那个……” 当然，那个邪恶的大臣对此非常不满，同时也觉得他的傀儡变得越来越不听使唤了；他开始考虑是否应该更换皇帝，但又不确定自己是否有能力成功实现这一计划。于是，他牵着一只鹿走进皇宫，叫皇帝出来，然后说道：‘看吧，陛下！我为您带来了一匹非常好的马！ 皇帝并不觉得这有什么好笑的，他回答道：‘你把鹿叫做马，肯定是弄错了吧？对吧？’” 过了一段时间，这个男人又重新结婚了，而他的新妻子对继女一点也不友善。但是，小女孩始终记得母亲的话，她总会躲到一个角落里，急切地照镜子——在镜子里，她仿佛看到了自己亲爱的母亲的容貌。那不是母亲临终时那张布满痛苦的神情，而是一张年轻而美丽的脸庞。 当屋主听到这个离奇的叙述后，他立刻去了女儿的房间。他突然出现在她面前，而女孩一看到他，立刻把镜子塞进了袖子里。这一次，她那宠爱她的父亲终于生气了，他开始怀疑妻子告诉他的那些话或许是真的，于是立刻把妻子的话复述了一遍。 当他的女儿听到这种不公正的指控时，她对父亲的话感到十分惊讶，于是告诉他说，她太爱父亲了，根本不可能也不会想要杀害他深爱的妻子。 "[rand |Long ago, there was a noble and righteous judge who was much loved by the people. One day, his magistrate understudy came up to him and asked: 'My lordship, how do you keep in favor with the emperor so consistently despite the workings of the court? Certainly you have angered many powerful people in your doings — how is it that you keep in his good graces, and hence his protection?" The judge considered his understudy, then replied to her: 'do you enjoy festival sweets?' 'Well, yes, my lordship.' The magistrate's reply was polite, but her hesitation betrayed her confusion. 'I'm truly looking forward to this summer for the chance to sample them again.' 'Could you have them every day, though?' 'No, the flavor is undoubtedly too rich. To have them every day... that would certainly make one ill.' 'And what of rice, then? What is so special about it that everyone has it everyday, without so much as thinking?' 'There is nothing special or noteworthy about it, my lordship. It simply fills the belly and keeps one going.' Several moments passed while the judge waited to see if his understudy would grasp the analogy, and when she did not he sighed and explained it to her. 'See, now. Every day, the emperor is plied not just by the twelve den mothers, but everyone in his court with the sweetest of deceptions. They may entertain him for a little while, but the empty compliments and transparent self-interest has him soon tiring of them; festival sweets are for the tongue and not the body. 'Yet I, with his permission, lay the simple truth before him when I am summoned to court. Like plain rice, it is not particularly exciting or tasteful, but my words are useful to him and he trusts me to give an honest assessment of any question he asks of me; in turn, I find that he reaches for my counsel as unthinkingly as people have rice every meal.'" Having finished her tale, Hotaru sets down her needle, steeples her fingers and smiles at you. "So, your thoughts about this tale[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" Sounds a bit contrived, but you understand that it's trying to get across a moral lesson.[pc.bg noblescion | You're well aware that in the world of aristocrats, it's not just as simple as telling the truth... ] "Mm. There is something I've noticed when looking over old Belharan tales and comparing them to that of my home nation. Where public officials are involved in folklore, those who star in tales were wicked ones who abandoned their duty. On the other hand, tales from across the ocean are of noble and righteous officials who at least tried to uphold the ideals of their station. "It says something about the times and places where these legends originated and the kinds of people they considered noteworthy[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. In old Belhar, people expected civil servants to at least try to do their jobs right. Not that it was necessarily the actual case, but the expectation was there, and wicked officials were considered noteworthy and enshrined in legend. On the other hand, righteous civil servants from my homeland were considered noteworthy of being immortalised in tales... which implies that people simply expected corruption and took it in stride if they were to meet with it." That... "Beautiful as it was, the period preceding the shogunate was a bit of a mess." Hotaru's smile turns sad. "I'd like to think we've learned something in all these centuries, to be in such a strong position compared to the other nations today. But there you have it[pc.ra kitsune |, my [pc.mf |lord |lady ]ship ] — a story for you." |This one's not from my homeland, but from neighboring Macah; nevertheless, I think it's a good enough story to tell. Long ago, there was a wicked prime minister in that land, who had installed a puppet emperor on the throne. Yet that was not good enough for him — said puppet emperor was chafing at his bonds due to a recent peasant uprising that was proving difficult to suppress, and not without reason blamed the prime minister for it. "Naturally, the wicked minister didn't like that, nor how uncooperative his puppet was becoming; he started to think that maybe there should be a change of emperor, but he couldn’t be sure he could pull it off. So he brought a deer into the palace by the horns, called the emperor to come out, and said: 'look, your majesty! I've brought you a fine horse!" "The emperor, not amused, replied: 'surely you are mistaken to be calling a deer a horse. Right?' "All the ministers in the court were on the edge of their seats; some were silently sweating nervously, while others loudly proclaimed what a fine horse this was. Great horse, look at this tail! These fine legs. Great horse, naturally the prime minister has the best of tastes. A handful did protest that this was a deer, not a horse; those were soon after summarily executed by some pretext or the other, and the emperor himself was mysteriously murdered some time later." Hotaru pauses a moment to let that all sink in, then shakes her head. "This story made it into the Records of the Grand Historian Sima Qian around three hundred years before the Godswar, through which it became part of common knowledge in Macahn intellectual life. From then on, every time somebody tried to pull off a similar stunt, opposing ministers could say 'you’re trying to say a deer is a horse, huh!.' That could either provoke other lukewarm ministers to wake up and support you... or get you killed with your whole family. "Such is the nature of these games[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. Bringing in a pony and calling it a horse won’t do; someone might honestly mistake a horse for a pony. Only lies that are breathtakingly stupid, things no sane person could say or believe, are sufficient to serve as loyalty tests for the wicked." Hmm. You remember a similar Belharan story about a child and the emperor's new clothes. Has she heard of that one? A small sigh. "I indeed have[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ] — taking in the native folktales has been interesting for a number of reasons. Such a tale: a child, who having a pure heart, dares to speak the truth against the powerful; the moral is that we should be ashamed of ourselves, and aspire to be as virtuous as this child. But of course the folktale abruptly cuts off there, because this child would have been arrested and executed in moments, along with his parents. It's plain why nobody tells the emperor about his new clothes: they’re not stupid." Gods, kitsune are downright depressing when they want to be. [pc.isDK |But... it's hard to argue with the thrust of the argument. How many inane self-deceptions do people labor under just to get through the day, let alone lies forced upon them by those around and above? |That folktale's meant to push an ideal, and just because it may be considered unrealistic by some, or that people fall short of it, doesn't mean that the ideal is worthless. Whether it's a good ideal to pursue shouldn't factor in the so-called realities of existence. ] "It is simply a different perspective, and the results of both are plain for all to see." |In ancient days there lived in a remote part of Kitsuhon a man and his wife, and they were blessed with a little girl, who was much beloved of her parents. On one occasion the man was called away on business by the coast. Before he went he told his daughter that if she were good and dutiful to her mother, he would bring her back a present she would prize very highly. Then the good man took his departure, mother and daughter watching him go. "At last he returned to his home, and after his wife and child had taken off his large hat and sandals he sat down upon the white mats and opened a bamboo basket, watching the eager gaze of his little child. He took out a wonderful doll and a lacquer box of cakes and put them into her outstretched hands. Once more he reached into his basket, and presented his wife with a metal mirror; its smooth surface shone brightly, while upon its back there was a design of pine trees and storks. "The good man's wife had never seen a mirror before, and on gazing into it she was under the impression that another woman looked out upon her as she gazed with growing wonder. Her husband explained the mystery and bade her take great care of the mirror. "Not long after this happy homecoming and distribution of presents, the woman became very ill. Just before she died, she called to her little daughter, and said: 'dear child, take care of your father when I am gone. You will miss me when I have left you, but take this mirror, and when you feel most lonely look into it and you will always see me.' Having said these words, she passed away. "In due time the man married again, and his wife was not at all kind to her stepdaughter. But the little one, remembering her mother's words, would retire to a corner and eagerly look into the mirror, where it seemed to her that she saw her dear mother's face, not drawn in pain as she had seen it on her deathbed, but young and beautiful. "One day, this child's stepmother chanced to see her crouching in a corner over an object she could not quite see, murmuring to herself. This ignorant woman, who detested the child and believed that her stepdaughter detested her in return, fancied that this little one was performing some strange magical art. Full of these notions, the stepmother went to her husband and told him that his wicked child was doing her best to kill her by witchcraft. "When the master of the house had listened to this extraordinary claim, he went straight to his daughter's room. He took her by surprise, and immediately the girl saw him she slipped the mirror into her sleeve. For the first time her doting father grew angry, and he feared that there was, after all, truth in what his wife had told him, and he repeated her tale forthwith. "When his daughter had heard this unjust accusation she was amazed at her father's words, and she told him that she loved him far too well ever to attempt or wish to kill his wife, who she knew was dear to him. 'What have you hidden in your sleeve?' said her father, only half convinced and still much puzzled. 'The mirror you gave my mother, and which she on her deathbed gave to me. Every time I look into its shining surface I see the face of my dear mother, young and beautiful. When my heart aches — and oh! it has ached so much lately — I take out the mirror, and mother's face, with sweet, kind smile, brings me peace, and helps me to bear hard words and cross looks.' "Then the man understood and loved his child the more for her filial piety. Even the girl's stepmother, when she knew what had really taken place, was ashamed and asked forgiveness. And this child, who believed she had seen her mother's face in the mirror, forgave, and trouble forever departed from the home." Having recited the entire tale, Hotaru reaches for a sip of tea while you ponder what she's just told you. For once, at least, a tale from a fox that doesn't end in misery, death, or any kind of horrible tragedy for anyone involved whilst teaching an important moral lesson. Even the antagonist in this learns to be better and lives contentedly instead of being miserably and horribly punished in a cruel and unusual fashion. "Oh, there're plenty of those, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |believe me ]," Hotaru says, setting down her teacup and returning to her needlework. "But sometimes, a little escapism from all the cynicism can't hurt." |Once upon a time there lived two frogs, one of whom made his home in a ditch near the coast, while the other dwelt in a clear little stream which ran through the mountains. At such a great distance apart, they had never even heard of each other; but, funnily enough, the idea came into both their heads at once that they should like to see a little of the world, and the frog who lived by the coast wanted to visit the inland mountains, and the frog who lived in the mountains wished to go to the coast and see the ocean for himself. "So one fine morning in the spring they both set out along the road that led from the coast to the mountains, one from one end and the other from the other. The journey was more tiring than they expected, for they did not know much about traveling, and halfway between their destinations there arose a traveler's stop which boasted a tall pavilion. It so happened that they decided to both take a rest within the rooftop garden, and what was the surprise of each to see another frog before him! "Both frogs looked at each other for a moment without speaking, and then fell into conversation, explaining the cause of their meeting so far from their homes. It was delightful to find that they both felt the same wish — to learn a little more of their native country — and as there was no sort of hurry they stretched themselves out in a cool, damp place, and agreed that they could learn much from each other before they parted to go their ways. "'What a pity we are not bigger,' said the coastal frog; 'for then we could see our destinations from here, and tell if it is worth our while continuing our journeys.' "'Oh, that is easily managed,' replied the mountain frog. 'We have only to stand up on our hind legs and hold onto each other, and then we can each look at the town he is traveling to.' "This idea pleased the coastal frog so much that he at once jumped up and put his front paws on the shoulder of his friend, who had risen also. There they both stood, stretching themselves as high as they could, and holding each other tightly, so that they might not fall down. The mountain frog turned his nose towards the coast, and the coastal frog turned his nose towards the mountains; but the foolish creatures forgot that when they stood up their great eyes lay in the backs of their heads, and that though their noses might point to the places to which they wanted to go, their eyes beheld the places from which they had come. "'Dear me!' cried the coastal frog, 'the mountains are exactly like the ocean. It is certainly not worth such a long journey, I shall go home!' "'If I had any idea that the coast was so alike to the mountains I should never have traveled all this way!' exclaimed the frog from the mountains, and as he spoke he took his hands from his friend's shoulders, and they both fell down on the ground. Then they took a polite farewell of each other, and set off for home again, and to the end of their lives they believed that the ocean and the mountains, which are as different as can be, were as alike as two peas." Having finished her story, Hotaru sets down her needlework and reaches for a little tea to wet her lips, studying you with her vivid red eyes and clearly awaiting a response. Well, what's the moral of the story? "Is there necessarily one[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]?" No, a story doesn't necessarily need to have a learning message, but given her method of delivery and the language she used in telling it, you get the feeling that this folktale about a couple of frogs is supposed to impart some kind of important lesson. It's a fox folktale, after all. "Mm, new experiences are good and all, but in order to benefit the most one needs to approach the new knowledge from a fresh perspective as well. Unable to change the way they saw things, the frogs benefited very little from their journey[pc.ra kitsune |, your Eminence ]. It's something to think about, and why I'm not particularly envious of those who travel." |Once, there was an old man named Takahama who lived in a little house behind a temple cemetery. He was extremely amiable and generally liked by his neighbors, though most of them considered him to be a little mad. His eccentricity, according to them, entirely rested upon the fact that he had never married or evinced desire for intimate companionship with anyone in all his years of life, preferring to remain a hermit. "One summer day he became very ill — so ill, in fact, that he sent for his sister and her son. Knowing that his neighbors considered him odd, they both came and did all they could to bring comfort during his last hours. While they watched, Takahama fell into a fevered asleep; but he had no sooner done so than a large white butterfly flew into the room and rested on the old man's pillow. His nephew tried to drive it away with a fan but it came back three times, loath to leave the sufferer. "At last Takahama's nephew chased it out into the garden, through the gate, and into the cemetery beyond, where it lingered over a woman's tomb, and then mysteriously disappeared. On examining the tomb the young man found the name 'Akiko' written upon it, together with a description narrating how Akiko died when she was eighteen. Though the tomb was covered with moss and must have been erected fifty years previously, the boy saw that it was surrounded with flowers, and that the little water tank had been recently filled. "When the young man returned to the house he found that his uncle had passed away, and he returned to his mother and told her what he had seen in the cemetery. "'Akiko?' replied his mother. 'When your uncle was young, he was betrothed to Akiko, but she died of consumption shortly before her wedding day. When Akiko left this world, your uncle resolved never to marry, and to live ever near her grave. For all these years he has remained faithful to his vow, and kept in his heart all the sweet memories of his one and only love. Every day he went to the cemetery, whether the air was fragrant with summer breeze or thick with falling snow; every day he went to her grave and prayed for her happiness, swept the tomb and set flowers there. When Takahama was dying, and he could no longer perform his loving task, Akiko came for him. That white butterfly was her sweet and loving soul.'" Having finished her tale, Hotaru gives you a quizzical look, then shakes her head. "There's no moral to be had here, [pc.ra kitsune |your Eminence |I'm afraid ]. It's just one of those slightly sad stories that people tell over a fire or lantern late at night." You didn't say there ought to be... "Mm." ] "
